requirements: Reproduce the core contributions of EPD-Serve: a stage-disaggregated multimodal inference serving system on Ascend that decouples Encode, Prefill, and Decode with asynchronous feature prefetching, hierarchical grouped KV transmission, modality-aware scheduling, and flexible physical co-location, achieving the reported throughput, TTFT, and TPOT improvements under SLO constraints.

sub_tasks.requirements: Set up the Ascend Atlas 800I A2 hardware environment, required software stack (vLLM v0.11.0 baseline, Mooncake Store, AISBench load generator), and reproducible experimental configuration.
Provision the Ascend Atlas 800I A2 hardware platform with the correct per-NPU memory and driver stack for reproducible experiments.
Code has been implemented to target an Ascend Atlas 800I A2 server as the execution platform, with configuration scripts or documentation specifying this hardware.
Code has been implemented to configure each Ascend NPU with 64 GB of on-device memory as reported in the paper's experimental setup.
Code has been implemented to install and load the Ascend CANN toolkit, driver, and PyTorch-Ascend runtime required to execute the Ascend NPU kernels used throughout the evaluation.
Code has been implemented such that a single-machine Ascend environment is used for all comparative evaluations under identical hardware configurations for fair comparison across deployments.
Install and configure the vLLM v0.11.0 baseline serving framework as the reference monolithic architecture for all comparative experiments.
Code has been implemented to install vLLM at version v0.11.0 (or a fork thereof adapted for Ascend) as the baseline monolithic serving system.

Code has been implemented such that the baseline configuration executes the Encode, Prefill, and Decode stages sequentially on the same computing resource, matching the monolithic vLLM behavior described in the paper.
Install and configure Mooncake Store to provide the asynchronous transmission and shared cache backend used by the E-P and P-D transmission mechanisms.
Code has been implemented to install and initialize the Mooncake Store, exposing its asynchronous transmission interface for use by the MM Store and KV transfer components.
Code has been implemented so that the Mooncake Store service is reachable from all Encode, Prefill, and Decode instance processes, providing a shared storage backend for cross-stage tensor transfer.
Set up the AISBench load generator to drive requests to the serving system at controllable per-NPU rates for evaluation.
Code has been implemented to install and invoke AISBench as the request injection tool that dispatches requests to the API server proxy of the serving system.
Code has been implemented so that AISBench supports controlled request rates in the 1-12 req/s range (per NPU) to simulate different concurrency levels used across the paper's experiments.

Code has been implemented such that per-NPU request rate is normalized by dividing the total dispatched rate by the number of NPUs in each deployment, ensuring a consistent single-device baseline for fair cross-deployment comparison.
Configure the reproducible experimental parameters (output length, SLO thresholds, deployment notation) shared across all evaluation scenarios.
Code has been implemented to fix the output sequence length to 64 tokens for every request across all experiments, as specified in the setup.
Code has been implemented to apply the SLO threshold TTFT ≤ 2000 ms and TPOT ≤ 80 ms when the Encode stage is disaggregated (and Decode is not), consistent with the paper's SLO convention.
Code has been implemented to apply the SLO threshold TTFT ≤ 2000 ms and TPOT ≤ 50 ms when the Decode stage is disaggregated, consistent with the paper's SLO convention.

Code has been implemented to parse and instantiate the deployment notation where '-' denotes disaggregation on separate hardware and '()' denotes physical co-location with logical isolation, supporting configurations such as TP1, TP2, (E-PD), E-PD, EP-D, (E-P)-D, (E-D)-P, and E-P-D.
Code has been implemented to record the four key evaluation metrics per experiment: SLO attainment rate, effective throughput (tokens/s per NPU), TTFT (ms), and TPOT (ms).
Prepare the VisualWebInstruct and ShareGPT-4o benchmark subsets with the exact sampling, resolution normalization, token-length statistics, and fixed output length used in the paper.

VisualWebInstruct subset preparation: acquire the source dataset and produce the exact 512-sample evaluation subset with correct modality split, image resolution normalization, and text-length statistics.

Code has been implemented to download or otherwise obtain the VisualWebInstruct dataset (Jia et al., 2025) from its official source and load it in a form that exposes both text prompts and associated images.
Code has been implemented that randomly samples 512 requests from VisualWebInstruct with a fixed random seed for reproducibility, producing a deterministic subset each run.
The VisualWebInstruct subset contains exactly 256 text-image (multimodal) requests and 256 text-only requests, and the code enforces this 50/50 split during subset construction.
Code has been implemented to standardize every image in the VisualWebInstruct subset to a resolution of 1280x720 pixels prior to serving requests to the inference system.
The average text input length across the prepared VisualWebInstruct subset matches the paper's reported statistic of 63.1 tokens (measured with the same tokenizer used by the target models).
ShareGPT-4o subset preparation: acquire the source dataset and produce the exact 512-sample evaluation subset with matching image resolution and text-length statistics.
Code has been implemented to download or otherwise obtain the ShareGPT-4o dataset (Chen et al., 2025) from its official source and load its text-image request pairs.
Code has been implemented that randomly samples 512 text-image requests from ShareGPT-4o with a fixed random seed, producing a deterministic subset each run.

The average image resolution across the ShareGPT-4o subset matches the paper's reported statistic of approximately 802x652 pixels (mean width x mean height), and images retain their native resolutions rather than being resized to a fixed target.
The average text input length across the ShareGPT-4o subset matches the paper's reported statistic of 9.6 tokens (measured with the same tokenizer used by the target models).
Global request generation configuration: enforce the paper's fixed output length and request injection controls used across all evaluations.

Code has been implemented so that every request submitted to the inference system uses a fixed output/generation length of 64 tokens (max_new_tokens=64) on both VisualWebInstruct and ShareGPT-4o subsets.

Code has been implemented that integrates AISBench (or an equivalent request-injection driver) to feed the prepared subsets into the serving system at configurable per-NPU rates in the range 1-12 req/s.
Code has been implemented that normalizes the per-NPU request rate by the number of NPUs used in each deployment configuration, so a common single-device baseline is applied when injecting requests.

openPangu-7B-VL acquisition and loading with correct component sizes.

Code has been implemented to download or otherwise acquire the openPangu-7B-VL model weights (ViT encoder plus autoregressive LLM decoder) from an accessible source and store them in a local model directory used by EPD-Serve.

Code has been implemented to load openPangu-7B-VL into the vLLM v0.11.0-based EPD-Serve runtime on Ascend, exposing separately addressable ViT (Encode) and LLM (Prefill/Decode) submodules so that stage disaggregation can be applied.
The loaded openPangu-7B-VL ViT component has approximately 0.7B parameters, matching Table 1.
The loaded openPangu-7B-VL LLM component has approximately 7B parameters, matching Table 1.
Qwen3-VL-8B acquisition and loading with correct component sizes.
Code has been implemented to download the Qwen3-VL-8B model weights (ViT encoder plus LLM decoder) from the official Qwen release and store them locally for use by EPD-Serve.

Code has been implemented to load Qwen3-VL-8B into the EPD-Serve inference runtime on Ascend, with the vision encoder and language model instantiated as separately schedulable modules to enable Encode/Prefill/Decode disaggregation.
The loaded Qwen3-VL-8B ViT component has approximately 0.6B parameters, matching Table 1.
The loaded Qwen3-VL-8B LLM component has approximately 8B parameters, matching Table 1.
Functional inference sanity for both loaded MLLMs.

Code has been implemented so that both openPangu-7B-VL and Qwen3-VL-8B accept image+text multimodal inputs and text-only inputs through the EPD-Serve API server proxy, producing decoded token outputs for a smoke-test request on each modality path.

A model registry / configuration entry has been implemented that identifies openPangu-7B-VL and Qwen3-VL-8B as the two evaluation models and wires them to the correct tokenizer, image processor, ViT hidden dimension, and LLM parallelism settings used by all downstream EPD-Serve experiments.

Implement the overall EPD-Serve architecture including API server proxy, per-stage instances (Encode/Prefill/Decode workers), schedulers, EP/PD connectors, and support for the deployment topologies E-P-D, EP-D, ED-P, E-PD, (E-PD).
The three-stage inference pipeline (Encode, Prefill, Decode) is decomposed into independent, separately schedulable modules with well-defined interfaces.

Code has been implemented that defines an Encode Worker module which loads only the multimodal encoder weights (ViT) and exposes an interface consuming multimodal inputs Im (images/audio/video) and producing embedding sequences Vm ∈ R^(n×d).

Code has been implemented that defines a Prefill Worker module which loads LLM weights, accepts text prompts It plus multimodal features Vm, concatenates them, and produces the first output token O1 along with KVCache KV1.

Code has been implemented that defines a Decode Worker module which loads LLM weights and autoregressively produces subsequent tokens (O_{t+1}, KV_{t+1}) = P(O_t, KV_t) until <eos> or the maximum generation length is reached.
Each stage worker runs as an independent process/instance with its own lifecycle and can be launched, terminated, and scaled independently without requiring the other stages to be co-instantiated.
The API Server Proxy front-end performs request ingestion, modality classification, and routing to the appropriate stage instances.
Code has been implemented that defines an API Server Proxy component exposing an HTTP/RPC entry point for inference requests and forwarding them to the internal scheduler layer.
The Proxy detects whether each incoming request contains non-text modalities (image/audio/video) and tags it as multimodal or text-only before routing.

The Proxy routes multimodal requests to the Encode entry of the E-P-D pipeline and text-only requests directly to the Prefill entry of the P-D pipeline, bypassing the Encode stage for text-only inputs.
Per-stage schedulers (Encode Scheduler, Prefill Scheduler, Decode Scheduler) manage request queues and dispatch to workers within each stage.
Code has been implemented that provides an independent Scheduler per stage (Encode/Prefill/Decode), each maintaining its own request queue and dispatch policy to its local worker(s).

A global instance status table tracks per-instance queue length, pending requests, and resource usage in real time, and is queried by the Proxy/schedulers to dispatch new requests to the least-loaded instance.
Cross-stage EP and PD connectors provide asynchronous tensor transmission channels between stage instances.

Code has been implemented that provides an Async EP Connector interface between Encode and Prefill workers responsible for transferring multimodal feature vectors and coordinating the hand-off via events.
Code has been implemented that provides an Async PD Connector interface between Prefill and Decode workers responsible for KVCache transmission with hierarchical/grouped scheduling hooks.
Each connector uses non-blocking asynchronous transfer primitives so that the sending stage does not block on the receiver's readiness handshake before continuing computation.
The system supports flexible disaggregation topologies through a unified deployment notation ("-" for disaggregation across NPUs, "()" for physical co-location with logical isolation).

Code has been implemented that supports a deployment configuration mechanism (config file or CLI flags) which accepts topology specifications such as E-P-D, EP-D, ED-P, E-PD, and (E-PD) and launches the corresponding worker layout.

The E-P-D topology places Encode, Prefill, and Decode on three separate NPUs with cross-NPU EP and PD connectors, and is verifiable via a launch that spawns three distinct worker processes bound to different NPU IDs.
The EP-D topology co-locates Encode and Prefill on the same NPU while Decode runs on a separate NPU, using local (intra-device) tensor hand-off for E→P and cross-NPU PD connector for P→D.
The (E-P)-D topology disaggregates Encode and Prefill on separate stage instances but co-locates them on the same NPU (logical isolation, physical sharing) while Decode occupies a separate NPU.
The (E-D)-P topology co-locates Encode and Decode on the same NPU (with logical isolation) while Prefill runs on a separate NPU.
The E-PD topology places Encode on a dedicated NPU while Prefill and Decode share another NPU (monolithic PD), with a cross-NPU EP connector for feature transfer.
The (E-PD) topology co-locates the Encode stage and the combined Prefill-Decode stage on the same NPU with logical isolation between them, using intra-device fast tensor exchange.
The TP1 and TP2 monolithic baselines (all three stages executing sequentially on 1 or 2 NPUs with tensor parallelism) are supported as reference deployments alongside the disaggregated topologies.
End-to-end data flow through the disaggregated pipeline correctly implements the sequence Encode → EP-transfer → Prefill → PD-transfer → Decode with proper token/KVCache dependencies.

When an end-to-end multimodal request is submitted under an E-P-D deployment, the system produces a token sequence terminating at <eos> or the max length, matching the semantics of the monolithic baseline on identical input.
Text-only requests skip the Encode stage entirely: the Encode Worker receives no work for such requests, and the request flows directly Proxy → Prefill → Decode with a PD-only transmission path.

Concatenation of multimodal feature vectors Vm and text feature Vt at the Prefill entry follows the ordering [Vm ; Vt] (or the model's expected order) so that generated outputs match the reference monolithic implementation on the same input.
The system integrates with the vLLM v0.11.0 code base as its serving foundation while extending it with the EPD disaggregation abstractions.
Code has been implemented such that the Prefill and Decode workers reuse vLLM's paged-attention KV cache management and model executor abstractions rather than reimplementing them from scratch.

The monolithic vLLM v0.11.0 configuration is preserved as a baseline that can be launched from the same repository, enabling side-by-side comparison with the disaggregated topologies on identical models and inputs.
Implement the E-P transmission mechanism with multimodal cache pooling (MM Store), event-driven asynchronous prefetching via hash keys, and fault-tolerant local recomputation.
Implement the MM Store multimodal cache pool for storing and retrieving encoded feature vectors keyed by input hashes.
Code has been implemented that defines an MM Store cache pool component (e.g., built on Mooncake Store) accessible from both Encode and Prefill instances.
Code has been implemented that computes a deterministic hash key from a multimodal input (image/audio/video bytes or preprocessed tensor) to serve as the MM Store lookup key.
Code has been implemented that stores encoded feature tensors V_m (shape [n, d]) into MM Store using the input hash as key after the Encode stage completes.
The MM Store deduplicates entries so that identical multimodal inputs (same hash) issued by concurrent or repeated requests are stored and transmitted at most once, enabling cross-request reuse.
Code has been implemented that on a Prefill instance retrieves the feature tensor from MM Store by hash and writes it into the local cache before Prefill computation begins.
Implement the event-driven asynchronous prefetching mechanism that sends hash events from Encode to Prefill and overlaps transmission with computation.
Code has been implemented as an EP Connector module that manages asynchronous E-P transmission between Encode and Prefill instances.
Code has been implemented that, once Encode finishes, sends only the lightweight feature hash (not the full tensor) as an event to the target Prefill instance.
Code has been implemented as an event listener on Prefill instances that receives hash events and triggers asynchronous feature fetch from MM Store.
Feature transmission is decoupled from Encode/Prefill computation using non-blocking asynchronous calls so that transfer and computation execute in parallel rather than serially.
Prefill scheduling waits (or polls) for feature availability using an event-completion signal rather than a blocking synchronous transfer, so scheduling latency can mask transmission latency.
The prefetch pathway supports both cross-node E-P transmission and physically co-located E+P deployment (feature move via shared memory / local MM Store) using the same interface.
Implement fault-tolerant local recomputation when the MM Store retrieval fails at the Prefill instance.
Code has been implemented that detects MM Store retrieval failure (miss, timeout, or transfer error) on the Prefill side for a given hash key.

Code has been implemented that, upon MM Store retrieval failure, triggers local re-execution of the multimodal encoder on the original input to regenerate the feature vector, preserving pipeline continuity.

The recomputation path produces feature tensors bit-equivalent (or numerically equivalent within model determinism) to those produced by the remote Encode instance, so downstream Prefill output is unchanged.
Validate the behavioral and measured performance characteristics of the E-P asynchronous prefetching mechanism.
A behavioral test verifies that enabling E-P asynchronous prefetching does not change the token outputs of the multimodal pipeline compared to a synchronous baseline (correctness preserved).
A behavioral test confirms that repeated requests with identical multimodal input reuse a single MM Store entry (cache hit path exercised, encoder not re-invoked on the second request).
Enabling E-P asynchronous prefetching (w/ E-P Asynchronous Prefetching vs Baseline E-P-D) on ShareGPT-4o reduces TTFT by approximately 16.6% at 2 req/s (Table 2, from ~703.75 ms to ~586.87 ms).
Enabling E-P asynchronous prefetching (w/ E-P Asynchronous Prefetching vs Baseline E-P-D) on ShareGPT-4o reduces TTFT by approximately 21.7% at 3 req/s (Table 2, from ~880.22 ms to ~688.86 ms).
For image resolutions up to 1080x1920, the E-P asynchronous prefetching mechanism achieves 100% transmission overlap ratio (feature transmission latency fully hidden by scheduling latency, Table 3).

At 4096x3112 resolution, the E-P asynchronous prefetching mechanism achieves an overlap ratio of approximately 99.78% (Table 3), with feature transmission latency slightly exceeding scheduling latency.
Implement layer-wise and hierarchically grouped KV cache transmission between Prefill and Decode with grouped packaging, asynchronous overlap, and precise scheduling.
Implement the layer-wise KV cache partitioning that emits KVCache produced by each Transformer layer as an independent transmission unit rather than one-shot end-of-Prefill transfer.

Code has been implemented that produces layer-wise KV transmission units per Transformer layer during Prefill, with a well-defined data structure/handle representing a single-layer KV payload (keys and values) ready for cross-instance transfer.

Code has been implemented so that when Prefill begins computation of the (L+1)-th layer, the KVCache from the L-th layer is dispatched for asynchronous transmission to the Decode instance (one-layer lag between compute and transmit).
The layer-wise transmission path uses non-blocking (asynchronous) send/receive calls so that Prefill computation of subsequent layers is not gated on completion of previous layers' KV transmissions.
Implement the hierarchically grouped KV transmission that packages adjacent-layer KVCache into groups, overlaps group transmission with MLP computation, and applies precise scheduling.

Grouped Packaging: Code has been implemented that packages KVCache from multiple adjacent Transformer layers into a single grouped payload for one transmission call, reducing per-layer handshake frequency.

Code has been implemented that determines the group size (number of layers per KV group) dynamically as a function of MLP compute load and measured/estimated metadata handshake latency, rather than a hard-coded constant.

Asynchronous Overlap: Code has been implemented with an event-driven queue that enqueues KV group transmission tasks and runs them in parallel with MLP computation of subsequent layers via producer/consumer semantics.

Code has been implemented for a metadata handshake step that is issued once per group (not per layer) and completes before/alongside MLP compute so that the handshake latency is masked by computation.

Precise Scheduling: Code has been implemented that defers/aligns KV group transmissions to avoid overlapping with peak communication phases (e.g., collective ops such as AllReduce), reducing link contention.

The transmission scheduler exposes hooks/events tied to specific compute milestones (e.g., MLP start/end of layer L) so that group transmission of layers L..L+g-1 can be issued at the intended alignment point.
Integrate the P-D transmission mechanism with the Prefill and Decode instances via the PD Connector using Mooncake's asynchronous transmission interface.

Code has been implemented for a PD Connector module on the Prefill side that submits grouped KV payloads for transmission and on the Decode side that receives them and populates the Decode KV cache prior to first Decode step.
The PD Connector uses the Mooncake asynchronous transmission interface (or an equivalent async RDMA-style API) as the underlying transport for KV group payloads.

Code has been implemented to preserve per-request KV ordering and correctness: the Decode instance can only begin token generation once all layer groups for that request have arrived and been written to its KV cache.
Provide profiling and measurement instrumentation for the P-D KV transmission pipeline to compute overlap ratio, exposed latency, and bandwidth utilization.

Code has been implemented that logs, per request, KV transmission latency, exposed (non-overlapped) latency, and Prefill computation latency so that overlap ratio = 1 - exposed/KV_latency (or equivalent definition) can be computed.

Code has been implemented to measure achieved transmission bandwidth (GB/s) for KV transfers by dividing transmitted payload size by transmission time for both baseline layer-wise and grouped variants.
Behavioral verification that the grouped/asynchronous mechanism actually overlaps communication with computation and reduces exposed latency versus a naive layer-wise baseline.

In a unit-style test with a controlled Prefill trace, disabling grouped/async transmission (baseline layer-wise mode) produces a substantially larger exposed transmission latency than enabling the hierarchically grouped mode, confirming overlap is functional.

Correctness check: KV tensors received on the Decode side under the grouped async path are numerically identical (elementwise) to those produced by a synchronous end-of-Prefill baseline transfer for the same inputs.

End-to-end TTFT reduction from the P-D hierarchically grouped mechanism alone (w/ P-D Hierarchically Grouped vs baseline E-P-D) on ShareGPT-4o is within tolerance of the reported 11.9%-16.0% range at 2 and 3 req/s.

At input sequence length 1024 with concurrency 16, the hierarchically grouped KV transmission achieves a KV overlap ratio close to the reported ~98.78% and improves over baseline layer-wise (~15.27%) by ~83.51 percentage points.

At input sequence length 2048 with concurrency 16, the hierarchically grouped KV transmission achieves a KV overlap ratio close to the reported ~99.92% and improves over baseline (~25.08%) by ~74.84 percentage points.

Measured average bandwidth utilization increases over baseline layer-wise transmission by approximately 58% at sequence length 1024 and approximately 10% at sequence length 2048, matching the paper's reported gains within tolerance.
Implement modality detection routing (E-P-D for multimodal, P-D for text-only) and instance-level dynamic load balancing based on a global instance status table.
Implement modality-aware multi-path routing that inspects each incoming request and dispatches it to the correct stage pipeline.

Code has been implemented in the API server proxy that inspects incoming requests and detects the presence of non-text modality fields (image, audio, video) versus text-only content, exposing a modality classification (e.g., 'multimodal' vs 'text-only') for the downstream router.

Code has been implemented that routes classified multimodal requests through the full Encode -> Prefill -> Decode pipeline, forwarding them first to an Encode instance before the request proceeds to Prefill.
Code has been implemented that routes text-only requests directly to the Prefill -> Decode pipeline, bypassing the Encode stage entirely so text requests never occupy Encode instances.

The routing layer keeps multimodal and text-only execution pipelines logically separated so that a burst of multimodal requests occupying Encode/Prefill instances does not prevent text-only requests from being dispatched to available Prefill instances (verifiable by unit test showing text throughput unaffected when Encode queue is saturated).
Implement the global instance status table and instance-level dynamic load balancing across Encode/Prefill/Decode instances.

Code has been implemented that maintains a global instance status table indexed by (stage, instance_id) storing at least the current queue length, number of pending/in-flight requests, and a resource-usage indicator (e.g., KV/MM cache occupancy) for every Encode, Prefill, and Decode instance.

Code has been implemented so that each stage instance reports updates (queue length, pending requests, resource usage) to the global status table in real time, and stale entries older than a configured threshold are refreshed or invalidated.

Code has been implemented that, when dispatching a new request to a given stage, queries the global status table and selects the instance with the lowest load according to a least-loaded-first policy (e.g., minimum queue length, with pending-request or resource-usage tiebreakers).

The least-loaded-first dispatcher demonstrably balances load across replicas: in a unit test with N homogeneous instances of a stage and M >> N sequential dispatches under equal service time, the maximum-minus-minimum request count across instances is at most 1.

The dispatcher prevents individual-node overload: in a stress test where one instance is artificially slowed, the scheduler shifts subsequent requests to less-loaded instances so the slow instance's queue length does not grow unboundedly beyond a configured cap.
Integrate modality-aware routing with instance-level load balancing so both operate together within EPD-Serve.

Code has been implemented so that after modality routing selects the target stage pipeline (E-P-D or P-D), the least-loaded-first selection is invoked per stage against only the instances belonging to that stage, and the chosen instance ID is passed to the transmission layer (E-P connector or P-D connector).

The scheduler exposes a configuration entry point (config file or CLI) allowing the operator to declare the number of Encode, Prefill, and Decode instances and their placement, and the router+balancer honor this topology when populating the status table and issuing dispatch decisions.

An end-to-end mixed-workload test (concurrent multimodal + text-only requests) confirms that (a) every multimodal request traverses Encode before Prefill, (b) every text-only request skips Encode, and (c) request distribution across replicas at each stage remains balanced within the tolerance defined by the load-balancer unit test.

Implement flexible stage disaggregation with elastic deployment, and physical co-location with operator-level spatial multiplexing across AI Core / AI Vector units for complementary operator scheduling.

Provide flexible stage disaggregation and elastic deployment: each of E, P, D stages runs as an independent instance process that can be scheduled and scaled separately, and instances can be distributed across nodes or co-located on the same node.
Code has been implemented that instantiates Encode, Prefill, and Decode as independent OS-level processes (or worker instances), each with its own scheduler and worker as depicted in Figure 3.
Code has been implemented that supports launching stage instances on the same NPU node (physical co-location) or on separate NPU nodes (disaggregation) via a deployment configuration.
Code has been implemented for a unified API Server Proxy component that performs cross-instance request routing and load balancing across Encode, Prefill, and Decode instances.
The system supports elastic scaling by allowing the number of instances per stage (E, P, D) to be configured independently at deployment time without recompiling.

A unified deployment notation is supported in configuration: '-' for disaggregated deployment of stages on separate hardware resources and '()' for logically isolated stages co-located on the same hardware (e.g., (E-PD), EP-D, (E-P)-D, (E-D)-P, E-P-D).

Code has been implemented that allows dynamic switching among deployment topologies (E-P-D, EP-D, ED-P, E-PD, etc.) by reconfiguring instance placement without requiring changes to model or scheduling code.
Inter-instance data transfer uses asynchronous communication interfaces (non-blocking send/receive) so that stage instances remain independently schedulable regardless of physical placement.

Support physical co-location and operator-level spatial multiplexing across AI Core and AI Vector units so that co-located stages can execute complementary operators in parallel and reclaim idle compute cycles.

Code has been implemented that allows two or more logically-isolated stage instances (e.g., E and PD, or E and D) to share a single NPU device while retaining independent process contexts and schedulers.

Code has been implemented that dispatches operators to AI Core versus AI Vector units on Ascend, exposing operator-level parallelism when co-located stages issue complementary operators (e.g., MatMul on AI Core, AllReduce/vector ops on AI Vector).

Under co-location, when one stage stalls on communication (e.g., data transfer or AllReduce), another co-located stage can proceed to issue compute operators, achieving temporal reuse of idle NPU cycles.

The co-location layer preserves logical isolation between stages (separate memory pools/streams so a fault or slowdown in one stage does not corrupt another's state) while sharing physical compute resources.

Provide a profiling / measurement utility that records per-operator latency when two operators from different stages run concurrently on the same NPU, producing the co-location interference heatmap shown in Figure 6 (right).

The measured operator-parallel interference heatmap shows that operator pairs with strongly differing resource requirements (e.g., an AI-Core-heavy MatMul co-located with an AI-Vector-heavy op) exhibit smaller latency inflation than pairs with similar resource demands.

Provide a per-operator resource-profile characterization (compute vs. data-movement proportion and AI Core / AI Vector usage) reproducing the left subfigure of Figure 6 for representative operators such as MatMul and AllReduce.
Integrate logical isolation with physical co-location so that deployment selection can be driven by workload characteristics, modality distribution, hardware availability, and SLO objectives.

Code has been implemented that treats each stage as an independent scheduling module at the software layer while permitting shared physical NPU allocation at the hardware layer, matching the logical-isolation + physical-co-location design described in Section 3.5.

Deployment configurations can be selected per SLO priority: (E-P)-D for balanced low TTFT + low TPOT, (E-D)-P for TTFT-critical workloads, and (E-PD) for throughput-maximizing workloads with relaxed latency.
The (E-PD) co-located deployment achieves measurably higher throughput than the TP1 monolithic baseline on openPangu-7B-VL at 12 req/s, with the reported improvement of 12.87-14.88%.

The (E-PD) co-located deployment reduces TPOT by 69.58-70.39% relative to TP1 on openPangu-7B-VL at 12 req/s, demonstrating the benefit of compute/memory complementarity between co-located E and PD stages.

The (E-D)-P co-located deployment reduces TTFT by 39.22-54.56% versus EP-D under high load, confirming that physical co-location of the compute-intensive Encode stage with the memory-intensive Decode stage improves first-token latency.
Reproduce the ablation on ShareGPT-4o at 2 and 3 req/s showing TTFT/TPOT for baseline (E-P-D), w/ E-P async prefetching, w/ P-D hierarchically grouped, and full EPD-Serve (Table 2).
Implement the ablation experiment harness that runs the four configurations (baseline E-P-D, w/ E-P async prefetching only, w/ P-D hierarchically grouped only, full EPD-Serve) on ShareGPT-4o.
Ablation configuration and toggling

Code has been implemented that exposes a configuration flag or toggle to enable/disable the E-P asynchronous feature prefetching mechanism independently of the P-D optimization, so the baseline path (synchronous, non-prefetched E-P transfer) can be reproduced.

Code has been implemented that exposes a configuration flag or toggle to enable/disable the P-D hierarchically grouped KV transmission independently of the E-P optimization, so a layer-wise synchronous P-D transfer baseline can be reproduced.

Code has been implemented that supports all four ablation configurations of Table 2 (Baseline E-P-D, w/ E-P Asynchronous Prefetching, w/ P-D Hierarchically Grouped, full EPD-Serve) as selectable experiment variants driven by CLI arguments or configuration files.

Each of the four ablation configurations, when launched with its selector, ends up running the same openPangu-7B-VL model, ShareGPT-4o workload, and E-P-D deployment topology, differing only in the two transmission-optimization toggles.
Workload injection at 2 and 3 req/s on ShareGPT-4o

Code has been implemented that drives the ShareGPT-4o 512-request subset through the EPD-Serve system at a configurable target request rate using AISBench (or an equivalent Poisson/rate-controlled injector), and supports the specific rates 2 req/s and 3 req/s used in Table 2.
Output length is fixed to 64 tokens for all requests in the ablation runs, matching the paper's uniform output-length setting.
TTFT and TPOT measurement pipeline
